aboutGame.title: What Is Build the Pyramids?
paragraphs: Build the Pyramids covers the engineering behind Egypt's Giza monuments, the three Fourth Dynasty tombs raised for Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure between roughly 2550 and 2490 BCE. Every guide here works from excavated evidence: quarry marks, tool assemblages, workers' villages, administrative papyri, and the monuments themselves.

Across 32 articles you can follow the whole chain of construction, from cutting limestone on the plateau and shipping granite 500 miles down the Nile to dragging blocks on wetted sand and lifting them up earthen ramps past 400 feet. The theories section weighs each competing explanation, hydraulic lifts, lost technology, and slave labour, against what the archaeological record actually shows.

modules.name: Build the Pyramids Beginner Guide
modules.description: A starting path through the Giza monuments: who ordered them, when they were raised, what they were for, and how the building crews were organised.

highlights.detail: Begin with the setting: Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure raised the Giza pyramids during Egypt's 4th Dynasty, between roughly 2550 and 2490 BCE.
Learn what a pyramid was for: a royal tomb and a solar stairway carrying the pharaoh's ka up to join the sun god Ra.
Meet the three monuments: the Great Pyramid at 481.4 ft, Khafre's at 471 ft, and Menkaure's at 218 ft.
See how the workforce was organised: 4,000 to 5,000 permanent specialists supported by 15,000 to 20,000 seasonal labourers.
Trace the materials from quarry to plateau: local limestone core, fine Tura casing, and Aswan granite from over 500 miles upstream.
Finish with the engineering: copper chisels, dolerite pounders, water-lubricated sledges, and earthen ramps climbing past 400 ft.

modules.name: Build the Pyramids Construction Methods
modules.description: The working construction model: quarrying, sledges on wetted sand, river barges, earthen ramps, and the surveying that fixed true north.

highlights.label: Quarrying
highlights.detail: Open-trench quarrying in the Giza bedrock produced rough core blocks averaging about 2.5 tons each.

highlights.label: Ramps
highlights.detail: Straight ramps served the lower courses, while zigzag and internal spiral ramps carried stone into the upper tiers.

highlights.label: Sledges
highlights.detail: Low wooden sledges on wetted sand cut sliding friction by roughly 50 percent, letting small crews haul 60-ton blocks.

highlights.label: Barges
highlights.detail: Sycamore-hulled cargo barges of 100 to 300 tons moved granite and Tura limestone along the flooded Nile.

highlights.label: Casing
highlights.detail: Fine white Tura limestone was fitted as the outer shell, giving the finished pyramid its smooth reflective face.

highlights.label: Alignment
highlights.detail: Builders fixed true north with shadow-casting gnomons and observations of the circumpolar stars.

modules.name: Build the Pyramids Great Pyramid Facts
modules.description: The headline numbers for Khufu's monument, from its original height and base length to its block count and internal chambers.

highlights.label: 481.4 ft
highlights.detail: Original height of Khufu's Great Pyramid, the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years.

highlights.label: 756 ft
highlights.detail: Length of each side of the base, laid out to within a fraction of a degree of true north.

highlights.label: 2.3M
highlights.detail: Estimated number of stone blocks in the Great Pyramid's core, casing, and internal chambers.

highlights.label: 5.75M tons
highlights.detail: Approximate total weight of the monument, raised over roughly 20 to 27 years of continuous work.

highlights.label: Khufu
highlights.detail: The Fourth Dynasty pharaoh, known to the Greeks as Cheops, for whom the Great Pyramid was raised.

highlights.label: Grand Gallery
highlights.detail: The 153-foot corbelled ascending hall that leads to the King's Chamber and its granite roof beams.

modules.name: Build the Pyramids Building Timeline
modules.description: A chronological walk from Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara to the three Fourth Dynasty monuments on the Giza plateau.

highlights.detail: About 2670 BCE: Djoser's Step Pyramid rises at Saqqara, the first pyramid, designed by the architect Imhotep as six stacked tiers.
Early 4th Dynasty: Sneferu's builders at Meidum and Dahshur work out the true smooth-sided pyramid after earlier collapses.
Circa 2550 BCE: work begins on Khufu's Great Pyramid at Giza, reaching 481.4 ft with roughly 2.3 million blocks.
20 to 27 years: the accepted construction window for the Great Pyramid, requiring about 100,000 blocks placed each year.
Circa 2520 BCE: Khafre adds the second Giza pyramid at 471 ft, sited on higher bedrock so it appears the tallest.
Circa 2490 BCE: Menkaure completes the plateau with a 218 ft pyramid finished in red Aswan granite.

modules.name: Build the Pyramids Workforce Guide
modules.description: The archaeology of the people who did the work: worker villages, rations, medical treatment, honoured burials, and the corvee system.

highlights.label: Workers
highlights.detail: Excavations at the Giza workers' village show paid, organised labour, not the enslaved workforce of popular myth.

highlights.label: Rations
highlights.detail: Crews were fed from on-site bakeries, breweries, and cattle butcheries that supplied thousands of workers daily.

highlights.label: Medical
highlights.detail: Skeletons show healed fractures and even successful trepanation, care that would never be given to expendable captives.

highlights.label: Burials
highlights.detail: Labourers were interred in honoured cemeteries beside the monuments they raised, a privilege denied to slaves.

highlights.label: Corvee
highlights.detail: Seasonal farmers worked off their corvee tax obligation during the Akhet flood, when their fields lay underwater.

highlights.label: Crews
highlights.detail: Workers were divided into named gangs under their own overseers, competing on quotas and recorded on papyri.

modules.name: Build the Pyramids Theories Ranked
modules.description: Competing explanations for how the pyramids were raised, ranked by how well each one holds up against the excavated evidence.

highlights.label: S
highlights.detail: Documented labour: worker villages, bakeries, medical care, and honoured cemeteries settle who built the Giza monuments.

highlights.label: A
highlights.detail: Ramp systems: straight, zigzag, and internal spiral ramps all leave archaeological traces and remain the leading model.

highlights.label: B
highlights.detail: Water-assisted transport: Nile flood canals and wetted sand are well supported, but internal hydraulic lifts stay debated.

highlights.label: C
highlights.detail: Alien construction: lost-technology claims rest on argument from incredulity and contradict every excavated tool assemblage.

modules.name: Build the Pyramids Tools and Materials
modules.description: The Old Kingdom toolkit and the stone it worked: copper chisels, dolerite pounders, quartz abrasives, and water-swollen wedges.

highlights.label: Copper chisel
highlights.detail: Unalloyed copper and arsenic-bronze chisels cut Tura limestone, re-forged on site as the edges dulled.

highlights.label: Dolerite ball
highlights.detail: Hard dolerite pounders crushed the Aswan granite that metal tools could not touch.

highlights.label: Quartz sand
highlights.detail: Quartz slurry let toothless copper saws grind through granite for sarcophagi and lintels.

highlights.label: Wooden wedge
highlights.detail: Dry acacia wedges driven into limestone cracks and soaked with water split blocks free from the bedrock.

highlights.label: Halfa rope
highlights.detail: Braided halfa grass and papyrus ropes, rated 2,000 to 8,000 lbs, harnessed the hauling gangs.

highlights.label: Cedar sledge
highlights.detail: Lebanese cedar and acacia sledges spread loads of up to 60 tons across wide wooden runners.

faq.title: Build the Pyramids FAQ
faq.description: Common questions about how the pyramids were built, answered from the archaeological record.

items.question: How long did it take to build the pyramids at Giza?
items.answer: Administrative documents and royal annals place the Great Pyramid at roughly 20 to 27 years. If Khufu's monument was finished in 23 years, crews quarried, moved, and set about 100,000 blocks every year to build the pyramids on that schedule.

items.question: Who built the pyramids?
items.answer: The builders were Egyptian. Excavations at the Giza workers' village uncovered barracks, bakeries, butcheries, and medical quarters, and the workers' cemeteries hold healed fractures and honoured burials. To build the pyramids, Egypt mobilised 4,000 to 5,000 permanent specialists plus 15,000 to 20,000 seasonal labourers during the Nile flood.

items.question: Were the pyramids built by slaves?
items.answer: The evidence does not support it. Skeletal remains show treated injuries and even successful brain surgery, care never given to expendable captives, and labourers were buried in cemeteries beside the monuments they raised. The crews who helped build the pyramids worked off a corvee tax obligation during the flood season.

items.question: What tools were used to build the pyramids?
items.answer: Old Kingdom builders had no iron. To build the pyramids they used unalloyed copper and arsenic-bronze chisels for limestone, dolerite pounding balls and quartz sand slurry for Aswan granite, and dry wooden wedges swollen with water to split blocks from the bedrock.

items.question: What stone was used to build the pyramids?
items.answer: Most of the bulk came from the plateau itself: rough nummulitic limestone averaging about 2.5 tons per block formed the core. Fine white Tura limestone, quarried across the Nile, was fitted as the outer casing, and pink Aswan granite from over 500 miles upstream faced the lower courses and roofed the King's Chamber. Every material used to build the pyramids moved by sledge, rope, and river barge.

items.question: Why were the pyramids built?
items.answer: They were royal tombs. In Old Kingdom belief the pharaoh was Horus incarnate on earth, destined to merge with Osiris after death, and the sloped faces worked as a stairway carrying his ka up to the sun god Ra. To build the pyramids was therefore both a burial project and a statement of cosmic order, or maat.
